title: Curing a whole leg ham at home
subtitle: Dry-curing a whole pig leg with salt and curing salts for long keeping.
excerpt: A whole leg ham is one of the most rewarding things to make from a home-killed pig. The process is methodical rather than difficult: the leg is rubbed with a dry cure of salt and curing salts, left to cure for several weeks in a cool space, then hung to dry for two to six months. The result is a dense, deeply flavoured cured ham that improves with age and can be sliced and eaten cold or cooked whole.
sourceNotes: Jane Grigson, Charcuterie and French Pork Cookery (1967), Penguin. Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall, The River Cottage Meat Book (2004), chapter on curing and preserving. Michael Ruhlman and Brian Polcyn, Charcuterie (2005), W. W. Norton, section on whole muscle cure techniques. UK Food Standards Agency, Guidance on the use of nitrites and nitrates in food (2023).

glossaryTerms.definition: A curing method where salt and curing salts are rubbed directly onto the meat surface rather than dissolved in a brine. The salt draws moisture out of the meat, creating a concentrated brine in situ.

A mixture of common salt and sodium nitrate or sodium nitrite (sodium nitrate is typically used for long cures). Curing salts inhibit the growth of Clostridium botulinum and other pathogens in cured meats and contribute to the characteristic pink colour and flavour.
A measure of the free water available in a food product. Dry curing reduces water activity to a level that inhibits bacterial growth, enabling long-term preservation without refrigeration.

content.text: A
dry-cured
whole leg ham requires a cool, stable environment (ideally 3 to 7 degrees Celsius), the correct quantity of
curing salt
, and patience. The curing period is not a set number of days: it scales with the weight of the leg. Plan on approximately two days of cure per kilogram of meat, plus resting time.

Curing salts containing sodium nitrate or nitrite must be used at the dosage specified by the supplier. Overdosing is a serious health risk. Use a proprietary blended cure (such as Cure No. 2 / pink salt for long dry cures) at the manufacturer's specified rate per kilogram of meat, not improvised mixtures.
Cure mix

A standard dry cure for a whole leg uses 30 g of fine sea salt per kilogram of meat, plus the manufacturer's specified dose of Cure No. 2 (long-cure pink salt) per kilogram. The salt draws out moisture, reducing the
water activity
of the meat and inhibiting bacterial growth. Additional flavourings, brown sugar, ground black pepper, dried herbs, are optional and can be added to the salt rub at 5 to 10 g per kilogram.
Initial cure
Weigh the leg. Calculate and weigh the precise cure amounts for the leg weight.
Rub the entire cure mix over every surface of the leg, including the cut face and around the hock, so that no meat surface is left uncoated.
Place the leg skin-side down in a non-reactive container (food-grade plastic, ceramic, or stainless steel). Spoon any excess cure mix from the container back onto the top of the meat.
Cover with a weighted board or plate and store at 3 to 7 degrees Celsius. Drain any liquid that accumulates in the container daily and flip the leg at the same time.
Cure for the calculated time (2 days per kilogram). A 10 kg leg needs 20 days of cure.
Resting and drying
After curing, rinse the leg under cold water and pat dry with clean cloths. Allow it to equalise in the refrigerator (uncovered) for 24 hours: the salt continues to distribute evenly.
Tie a hanging string around the hock and hang the ham in a cool, well-ventilated space. A cool shed or outbuilding at 8 to 15 degrees with air circulation is the traditional environment.

A mould bloom on the surface of the skin is normal and expected. Wipe with a cloth dampened in a dilute white wine vinegar solution if the mould is heavy. Grey-green surface mould on the skin is benign; black mould or mould penetrating the flesh is not.
Minimum hanging time is 2 months; traditionally 4 to 6 months is preferred. A probe inserted to the centre of the thickest part of the ham should smell clean and meaty, not off or sour.

attrs.cue: The centre of the ham smells off when probed
attrs.cause: Insufficient salt penetration at the bone joint (femoral artery pocket), or curing temperature too high
attrs.fix: If the off smell is near the ball-and-socket joint, this is bone taint from inadequate curing at the deep joint. The ham is not safe to eat and must be discarded. Prevention: make a small injection of saturated brine into the hip joint on day 1 of curing.

attrs.cue: Ham is extremely salty when tasted
attrs.cause: Over-cured or salt did not fully equalise
attrs.fix: Soak the ham in cold water for 12 to 24 hours before cooking, changing the water twice. This draws out excess surface salt.
